title: Karkotaka's bite
hookLine: Nala carries a snake king out of a fire, and its bite starts driving out the Kali inside him
carry: reciting nala's story is a prayer against kali

cards: A voice in a forest fire. Nala, wandering alone after leaving Damayanti, hears someone calling his name out of the flames. Come quickly, Nala.
He follows the voice and finds, curled in the fire, a great serpent. It's Karkotaka, a king among the nagas, and he can't move: a sage's curse has frozen him there until Nala comes to carry him.
So the man who lost everything at dice lifts a snake king onto his shoulder and walks out of the fire. And then the snake bites him.

teach.b: Nala's body changes. His beauty is gone; no one would know him now. And Karkotaka explains: my poison won't hurt you.
It will torment the one living inside you, the one who brought all this on you. That's Kali. Not the goddess Kali; a different name.

teach.h: KALI, THE SPIRIT OF BAD LUCK.
teach.b: This Kali is the spirit of quarrel and bad luck, the same name Hindus give our whole age, the Kali Yuga.
Then the serpent gives Nala a plan. Go to King Rituparna of Ayodhya. Call yourself Vahuka and drive his horses, and he'll teach you his secret of dice.
And take this garment: when you want your own shape back, put it on and think of me. So the king becomes a charioteer. Every evening he recites a lament for a woman left alone in a forest.

Meanwhile, Damayanti has been found and brought home to her father's house and her children. She sends Brahmanas out with one question for every court: where did you go, gambler, after you cut your sleeping wife's cloth?

teach.h: FOUR NAMES THAT DRIVE OUT KALI.
teach.b: With this story comes a short Sanskrit verse, still recited, that names four people: Karkotaka the serpent, Damayanti, Nala, and the royal sage Rituparna. Naming them, it says, destroys Kali.
Notice who comes first: the snake whose bite began to drive Kali out. Some Hindus still say the verse in a hard season, a lost job, an illness, a run of bad luck.
For today: in this tradition, a story isn't only something you hear.

teach.h: A STORY, SAID AS A PRAYER.
teach.b: Said with faith, it's a prayer.

how: In the Mahabharata's Nala story, the serpent Karkotaka disguises Nala and torments Kali inside him; a verse with the story names Karkotaka, Damayanti, Nala and Rituparna as destroying Kali, and some Hindus still recite it in hard times.

o: the charioteer name Nala takes in Ayodhya
the king of Ayodhya who knows the secret of dice
the serpent king whose bite hides Nala

games.q: Nala in hiding — tap the pairs.
p: bites Nala and changes his shape
king of Ayodhya, who knows dice

s: Karkotaka's poison was meant to kill Nala
it was meant to torment Kali inside him and hide Nala, not harm him.
Karkotaka gave Nala a way to get his shape back
a garment to put on when he wanted his own form, thinking of the serpent.
the Kali in Nala's story is the goddess Kali
a different name: Kali, the spirit of quarrel and bad luck, who gives the Kali Yuga its name.

games.q: you're Nala. Karkotaka's poison is in you and you feel changed. what does the serpent say it's doing?
o: hiding you, and tormenting Kali inside you.
nothing; the bite was an accident.
games.why: the poison works on Kali, not on Nala. that's why Karkotaka is the first name in the verse said against Kali.

practice: Say the four names of the verse slowly, one on each breath out: Karkotaka. Damayanti. Nala.
Rituparna. Let each one bring back a piece of the story: the bite, the search, the hiding, the secret of dice.
If you pray, hold a hard season of your own, or someone else's, in that prayer; if not, simply bring to mind the people who carried you through one.

wordCard.voice: Karkotaka. The naga king whose bite hid Nala and tormented Kali, and the first name in the verse said against Kali.

orig.note: Sanskrit Karkotaka, the naga king who disguises Nala with his bite.

carryVoice: Your line: reciting Nala's story is a prayer against Kali. A snake king, named first. Day seven hundred ninety-three, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Nalopakhyana: Karkotaka in the fire; the bite; Nala as Vahuka in Rituparna's service; Damayanti found and brought home; Damayanti sends Brahmanas with her question; the closing verse naming Karkotaka, Damayanti, Nala and Rituparna as destroying Kali)
